title: Game Theory
subtitle: Game theory models situations in which your outcome depends on the choices and expectations of others.

blocks.text: Game theory models situations in which your outcome depends on the choices and expectations of others.

Game theory models situations in which your outcome depends on the choices and expectations of others. The beginner’s job is not to master the field in one sitting. It is to learn the field’s central question, the few concepts that explain most of its value, and the situations in which its lens changes a decision.

Human beings encounter problems related to game theory that ordinary intuition handles imperfectly. Game Theory exists as a disciplined way of describing patterns, testing explanations, building useful models, or making choices under the field’s characteristic constraints.
1. Payoffs

Think of payoffs as one of the field’s high-leverage ideas. In beginner language, it is a way of noticing a pattern that can otherwise remain hidden. The important move is to ask what the concept lets you predict, compare, or explain that ordinary intuition might miss.

rows: Imagine a familiar situation involving game theory where payoffs changes the outcome.
The concept gives you a better question to ask and a better way to distinguish competing explanations.

blocks.text:
INNER SECRET
Your action changes the incentives and expectations of the other player.

WAIT… REALLY?
A stable equilibrium can be collectively bad.

Experts in game theory do not merely know more facts. They notice structure earlier. They define the problem carefully, choose an appropriate level of analysis, identify assumptions, compare alternatives, and know when a familiar model has reached the edge of its useful range.
Beginner Thinks / Expert Notices
BEGINNER THINKS: the visible event is the explanation. EXPERT NOTICES: the mechanism, context, incentives, interactions, evidence quality, and boundary conditions behind the event.

blocks.text:
TOOL
FIELD LENS: define the problem → choose the relevant concepts from game theory → identify assumptions → make a prediction or comparison → test against evidence → revise.
Choose one ordinary situation today and deliberately look at it through the lens of game theory. Write three observations: what you noticed, what you initially assumed, and what the new lens added.

Use one idea from game theory to improve a real decision, process, explanation, or conversation. State the original approach, the new approach, and what evidence would tell you whether the change helped.

WATCH OUT
Game Theory is not a magic decoder ring. A useful framework can improve reasoning without guaranteeing a correct prediction in every context.

Every model compresses reality. The right response is not to abandon models but to ask what assumptions they require, what they omit, how context changes them, and what another discipline might reveal.

items: Game Theory ↔ Systems Thinking: compare the level of analysis, the type of evidence, and the kind of question each field makes easier to answer.
Game Theory ↔ Complexity: compare the level of analysis, the type of evidence, and the kind of question each field makes easier to answer.

Answers / Reflection Guide
Game theory models situations in which your outcome depends on the choices and expectations of others.
The most useful concept is the one that changes what you can notice or test in a real situation.
The framework has assumptions and should not be treated as a complete description of reality.
Interdisciplinary analysis is strongest when the second field adds a genuinely different mechanism or level of explanation.
